defects.why: يتداخل هذا المقطع مع درس المسار الآخر «قبل النوبة: الجوع والنعاس والانتقال المفاجئ» الذي يغطي الجوع والنعاس والانتقال المفاجئ قبل النوبة، فيضعف تميّز الدرس.
تغفل هذه القائمة علامة الخطر «يصعب تهدئته» الواردة في وحدة المعرفة؛ فقد يحتاج الطفل الذي يصعب تهدئته إلى تقييم طبي حتى لو لم يؤذِ نفسه أو لم تكن النوبات شديدة ومتكررة.
صياغة إنجليزية متكلفة؛ الترجمة الأدق لعبارة «هدوء سريع» هي quick calm.

defects.why: استخدام «عليه» بعد «شعور قوي» غير دقيق وقد يوحي بأن الشعور ضدّه؛ الأصوب «لديه» أو «يغمره».
«لتنتهي النوبة» قد تُفهم خطأً أن الغاية أن تنتهي النوبة وليس أن تغيير القرار هو الوسيلة؛ الأوضح «لإنهاء النوبة».
«صرف انتباهك عنه» تركيب ملتبس؛ قد يُقرأ «صرف انتباهه عنك» والأوضح «أمّا تجاهلك إيّاه».

lessons.brief: بعد أن يهدأ: الحضن أولًا ثم الكلمات

defects.why: الضمير «ها» يعود على «لمسة» المؤنثة فقط، فيُفهم أن الشرط خاص باللمسة دون الحضن، والصواب أن يشمل الاثنين.
الدرس مخصص لما بعد نوبة الغضب الكاملة، لكن try_this يقول «أول لحظة غضبٍ أو بكاءٍ» وهو أوسع نطاقًا وقد يطبّق على انفعال بسيط لا يستدعي كل هذه الخطوات، ما يخلّ بدقة الربط بين الملخص والفعل المطلوب.

lessons.title: بعد أن يهدأ: الحضن أولًا ثم الكلمات

defects.why: The Arabic says «ولا أنك أخطأت في تربيته» — 'made a mistake/erred in raising him' — which is gentler than 'failed in raising them'. 'Failed' overstates the Arabic and adds a tone of finality not present in the original.
«أيّ» صيغة مذكّرة، والصواب مع «القصّتين» المؤنثة «أيّة القصّتين».
صياغة متكلّفة بعض الشيء؛ الأوضح «كثير المطالب وصعب الإرضاء».
ينكسر تسلسل الزمن في السؤال: سبقها مضارع «يتألّم» ثم جاءت «بدا» ماضية، والصواب «يبدو» للمطابقة.
الكلمة اسم مفعول من أحبط وتُكتب «مُحبَط» بضم الميم؛ ورودها دون الضمة قد يُقرأ خطأ.

The action assumes another caregiver exists and is available today. A parent who is the sole caregiver (e.g., alone at home with the child) cannot perform this action as written, making it not universally doable today.

lessons.brief: نوبةٌ في السوق أو أمام الضيوف

defects.why: The phrase 'فتتّجه إليك الأنظار' is slightly stiff and literary for a warm, direct parenting read. A more natural MSA phrasing would be 'فقد تتجه إليك الأنظار' or 'فينظر إليك الناس'.
The phrase 'تغضب عليه' is slightly colloquial in this context. In MSA, 'تغضب منه' or 'تصرخ عليه' is more precise. The lesson itself later uses 'ولا تصرخ عليه'.
The word 'متألم' is less common in everyday MSA than 'يشعر بألم'. It is not incorrect, but slightly stiff.
The phrase 'ولا تَعِده بحلوى' is grammatically correct but slightly awkward. 'ولا تعده بالحلوى' or 'ولا تعده حلوى' flows better.
The phrase 'فليبقَ هو معه' is grammatically correct but sounds stiff and formal. A warmer phrasing would be 'فدعه يبقى معه' or 'فليبقَ معه'.
The word 'حساب' (reckoning) is a bit strong and preachy. 'عتاب' (blame) or 'لوم' (blame) is softer and more appropriate for a parenting context.
The action is concrete and doable, but it combines two distinct actions (telling + giving a task). The instruction says 'ONE concrete action'. This is a minor violation.

The Arabic says 'وقدّم نومه ولو فاتتك بعض الأمور' which means 'prioritize his sleep even if you miss some things'. The English 'put their sleep first' is a direct translation, but the Arabic uses the singular 'نومه' (his sleep) referring to the child, while the English uses 'their'. This is a minor inconsistency but not a meaning change. However, the phrase 'ولو فاتتك بعض الأمور' is more naturally 'even if it means missing out on some things' in English. The current translation is acceptable.

The Arabic 'تغضب عليه' is translated as 'lose your temper with them', which is a good idiomatic equivalent. However, the Arabic later uses 'ولا تصرخ عليه' (do not shout at him), and the English uses 'shouting at them'. The consistency is fine.
The English 'feel your own temper rising' is slightly more idiomatic than the Arabic 'اشتدّ انفعالك' (your emotion intensifies). This is a good translation choice.
The Arabic uses «سنشتري الخبز والحليب، ولن نشتري الحلوى اليوم». The English translation is accurate and maintains the quotation marks.

lessons.title: نوبةٌ في السوق أو أمام الضيوف

defects.why: The phrase 'فحاول أن تلاحظ' is slightly stiff and preachy. A warmer, more direct phrasing would be 'حاول أن تلاحظ' without the فاء, or 'لاحظ انزعاجك'. Also, 'بضعة أنفاسٍ عميقة' is grammatically correct but 'بضعة' is less common in easy MSA; 'خذ أنفاسًا عميقة قليلة' or 'خذ ثلاثة أنفاس عميقة' would be smoother.
The phrase 'ترفق فيها بنفسك' is slightly awkward. 'كن رفيقًا بنفسك' or 'ارفق بنفسك' is more natural in MSA.
The passive form 'يُصلَح' is grammatically correct but sounds stiff. 'كيف يُصلِح الخطأ' (active) is more natural and aligns with the child learning to fix mistakes.

The phrase 'وأنت قريبٌ من طفلك' is slightly ambiguous. It could mean 'while you are close to your child' which is fine, but 'وأنت بجانب طفلك' or 'وأنت مع طفلك' is warmer and clearer. Also, 'فادعُه' is grammatically correct but 'فادعه' without the damma is more common in modern writing.

The Arabic says 'وإن احتجت وقتًا أطول، كأن تمشي قليلًا، فلا تتركه وحده: اجعل شخصًا تثق به يرعاه حتى تعود.' The English 'such as a short walk' is a direct translation, but the Arabic 'كأن تمشي قليلًا' implies 'like taking a short walk' which is a suggestion, not a strict example. The meaning is preserved, but the tone is slightly more prescriptive in English. However, the main issue is that the English omits the nuance of 'كأن' which is a hypothetical example, not a definitive one. This is minor.

The English 'Take moments to be gentle with yourself' is a bit stiff and clinical. The Arabic 'وخذ لحظاتٍ ترفق فيها بنفسك' is warmer. A more natural English phrasing would be 'Take some moments to be kind to yourself'.

The English 'how a mistake is put right' is passive and stiff. The Arabic 'كيف يُصلَح الخطأ' is also passive, but the English could be more active and natural: 'how to put a mistake right' or 'how to fix a mistake'.

The English 'while staying close to your child' is slightly clinical. The Arabic 'وأنت قريبٌ من طفلك' is warmer. 'while you are close to your child' or 'while you are with your child' would be more natural.

primary_sources.used_for: AAP (served as 'Top Tips for Surviving Tantrums'): tantrums normal; do not ignore hitting, kicking, biting, throwing; stop it immediately; hold a child in danger; distraction; give yourself a break; talk with your pediatrician
AAP: spanking, yelling and shaming harmful; parent's own time-out with the child in a safe place, then hug and start over; never take away something the child truly needs
AAP: anger erupts as tantrum, may hit, bite or kick; consult pediatrician if very withdrawn, perpetually sad, or highly demanding and unsatisfied most of the time

AACAP: tired, hungry, pain, mild illness; remain calm (modeling); words not unsafe actions; distraction; state calmly which behaviour must stop; never physically aggressive; seek help for danger, self-harm, not calming, very frequent/longer than expected, interfering with life (minute figures not used)
CDC: ignoring only for minor safe attention-seeking behaviour (whining); never needs-based, distress or danger; do not leave alone unless safe; return attention when it stops

CDC: ensure safety, remain close, hands free, time and space; wait until both calm; notice, connect (eye contact, smile, touch), name the emotion, accept correction; validate feelings and limit behaviour; do not rush to solutions; parent's pause or another trusted caregiver
CDC: giving in rewards the tantrum; spanking, yelling and embarrassing are unhealthy; go back to being positive
CDC: teach acceptable ways to show they are upset; praise positive behaviour
CDC: lost skills or other concerns -> talk with the child's doctor

NHS: find out why (tired, hungry); shouting back will not end it; do not change your mind or bribe with sweets; distraction; holding when more upset than angry and you are calm; do not hit back, make clear hitting hurts; 'I know you're feeling angry'; praise and cuddles; GP if seriously concerned
